one_liner: Go Reed-Solomon erasure coder with generated SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512/GFNI, NEON/SVE and ppc64le kernels; 5-19x its own pure-Go path.
what_it_does: Computes parity shards over GF(2^8) for k data + m parity byte slices and reconstructs up to m missing shards (Encode, Verify, Reconstruct, ReconstructData, ReconstructSome), with Split/Join helpers, a streaming io.Reader/io.Writer API, progressive EncodeIdx/DecodeIdx and Update. It is a Go port of Backblaze's JavaReedSolomon (same Vandermonde matrix and output), with Cauchy, Jerasure-compatible, PAR1, XOR-only and custom matrices as options. Above 256 total shards (or on request) it switches to a Leopard-RS-compatible O(N log N) FFT codec in GF(2^8) or GF(2^16) for up to 65,536 shards.
how_it_is_fast: The x86 kernels use the split-nibble table method from 'Screaming Fast Galois Field Arithmetic' (two 16-entry tables applied with PSHUFB/VPSHUFB), and on AVX-512/AVX GFNI CPUs a GF2P8AFFINEQB 8x8 bit-matrix per coefficient instead of table lookups. avo programs in _gen generate one fused kernel per (inputs x outputs) shape up to 10x10 (mulAvxTwo_10x4_64, mulGFNI_..., mulNeon_10x10), so every input block is loaded once and all parity outputs stay in registers; larger shapes are tiled in 10x10 blocks sized to L1/L2 (perRound from cpuid cache sizes). CPU features are detected at run time through klauspost/cpuid, and the Leopard mode replaces O(k*m) matrix multiplication with additive FFTs.
when_to_use: Go storage or transport code (object stores, backup, FEC over UDP) that needs k+m erasure coding with k+m up to 256 and shards of tens of KB or more, where it runs at tens to hundreds of GB/s per encoder.
amd64 servers with AVX2, and especially AVX-512 plus GFNI, where the GFNI kernels reach 241-274 GB/s on the README's 5+2, 8+8 and 10+4 rows.
arm64 servers (Graviton, Kunpeng, Apple) via generated NEON and SVE kernels, and ppc64le via its own assembly (about 9x over pure Go in the README).
Very wide codes (hundreds to 65,536 shards) via the Leopard GF16 mode, or 20+ shards via WithLeopardGF(true) when encode speed matters more than reconstruction speed.
When byte compatibility with Backblaze JavaReedSolomon, reed-solomon-erasure (Rust) or the Jerasure matrix layout is required.
when_not_to_use: C or C++ projects: this is a Go package with Go-ABI assembly; the README links reedsolomon-c (a compatible C port) but makes no comparison with Intel ISA-L (intel/isa-l, catalogued separately), the usual C baseline.

Platforms without its assembly (riscv64, s390x, wasm, 386) or builds with -tags=noasm: these run the pure-Go table path, which for fewer than 20 total shards lazily builds a 32 MiB two-byte multiplication table (mulTable16, 256 x 65536 uint16).
Reconstruction-heavy Leopard workloads: Leopard GF16 encodes 5.6-27 GB/s but recovers only 1.2-3.2 GB/s in the README table, and the reconstruction-matrix cost cannot be cached at high shard counts.
Data-integrity detection: the encoder cannot tell which shard is corrupt; callers must hash each shard and pass known-bad ones as nil.

Short-lived encoders: New() builds matrices and pools, and issue #319 (Kunpeng-920) showed a 33% throughput drop with one encoder per call under heavy concurrency; the maintainer says encoders are meant to be reused.

integration.dependencies: github.com/klauspost/cpuid/v2 (golang.org/x/sys indirect); avo only to regenerate the amd64 assembly (_gen module)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.24 (go.mod go 1.24); CI tests Go 1.24.x, 1.25.x and 1.26.x
integration.platforms: amd64 (SSE2/SSSE3/AVX2/AVX-512/GFNI, runtime dispatch), arm64 (NEON, SVE), ppc64le (assembly); pure Go elsewhere (CI runs 386 tests). CI covers Linux, macOS, Windows and ubuntu-24.04-arm.
integration.thread_safety: Not stated in the README or Encoder doc; the repo's BenchmarkParallel and the maintainer's reply in issue #319 share one encoder across goroutines, and the inversion cache is guarded by an RWMutex. Encode itself fans out to internal goroutines (WithMaxGoroutines, WithAutoGoroutines).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the pure-Go path is the same package with SIMD switched off (WithAVX2(false) and similar), so the speedup is automatic; it does not replace other erasure-coding libraries unless their matrix layout matches (Backblaze, Jerasure and custom matrices are supported).

gotchas: Harness asymmetry behind the README table: New() caps the goroutines that split one Encode call at codeGenMaxGoroutines = 8 when the AVX2 code-gen path is usable and at gfniCodeGenMaxGoroutines = 4 when GFNI is, while the pure-Go and SSSE3 paths get maxGoroutines sized by WithAutoGoroutines (rounded up to a multiple of GOMAXPROCS and usually 2x GOMAXPROCS, so 64 at the table's 32 threads). So '32 threads' describes GOMAXPROCS, not the workers each column used, and the per-core gain of AVX2/GFNI over pure Go is larger than the 5-19x wall-clock ratios. This favours the baseline, so the claim is not inflated, but the columns are not equal-thread comparisons.

Methodology gaps: no CPU model, Go version or command line is given (README benchmark names carry a -32 GOMAXPROCS suffix and a New() comment tunes a switchover 'for Zen5', but neither names the test CPU); MB/s counts data plus parity bytes, so data throughput is lower by k/(k+m); the same 7-70 MB of buffers are re-encoded in place, so the 5+2, 8+8 and 10+4 rows may be cache-resident on a large-L3 part while 50+20 (70 MB) is memory-bound, which fits GFNI gaining only 7% over AVX2 there. The README also does not say whether the AVX2 column disabled the separate AVX+GFNI path (-no-avx-gfni).

Several releases were retracted or patched for crashes, not wrong output: v1.11.6 slice-bounds panic in codeSomeShardsAVXP (issue #240), v1.12.2 Graviton4 build (PR #283), a ReconstructSome segfault from PR #267 fixed in PR #303 (issue #302), an arm64 NEON out-of-bounds read in mulNeon_10x10 fixed in v1.13.3 (#329), a SIGILL on GFNI CPUs without AVX-512 fixed in v1.13.2 (#325), and a GFNI-on-non-GFNI-CPU test crash reported by Debian fixed in v1.14.2 (#343/#344).

The checked-in amd64 assembly cannot currently be regenerated from scratch (issue #346, open: deleting galois_gen_amd64.s breaks go generate), and -tags=nopshufb (the README's patent mitigation) removes the PSHUFB kernels, so CPUs without GFNI fall back to the pure-Go path with its 32 MiB table.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The Go-assembly siblings (cespare/xxhash, lukechampine/blake3, zeebo/blake3, go-and, pospop, minio/md5-simd) solve hashing, bitwise and popcount problems; pick this one when a Go program needs erasure coding, where it is the de facto SIMD implementation. Like those siblings its headline ratio is asm versus the same package's pure-Go path, not versus a C library such as ISA-L.
verified_claims_summary: The README Performance table, refreshed in PR #336 (2026-04-21), encodes 1 MB random shards with GOMAXPROCS 32 on an unnamed x86 CPU with an unstated Go version: pure Go 3.5-40.7 GB/s versus AVX2 44.7-202 GB/s (4.97x for 5+2 up to 12.7x for 50+20) and AVX-512 GFNI 47.7-274 GB/s (5.94x to 19.1x), with throughput counted over data plus parity bytes (ratios derived from page data). Per-call goroutine caps (8 for AVX2, 4 for GFNI, about 2x GOMAXPROCS for pure Go) mean the SIMD columns used fewer cores than the baseline.
status_note: Actively maintained (v1.14.2 released in August 2026, last commit 2026-09-25, CI on three Go versions and four OS targets) and MIT-licensed; widely used, with a history of crash fixes and retracted releases but no reported wrong-parity bug in the issues reviewed.
